opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the commitment problem is one of the core puzzles in cooperation, and I think it's one of the most important for thinking about how advanced AI could go well or badly.

The basic idea is that there are many situations where two or more parties would all be better off if they could reach some agreement, but they can't credibly commit to sticking to it. Because they can't trust each other to follow through, they end up in a worse outcome than they could have gotten. The classic example from international relations is war. War is costly. In principle there's almost always some bargain, some division of territory or resources, that both sides would prefer to actually fighting. So why do wars happen? A big part of the answer, going back to work by James Fearon and others, is that parties can't credibly commit. If I'm rising in power and you're declining, I might promise to treat you well later, but you know that once I'm stronger I'll have every incentive to renege. So you may prefer to fight now, while you still can, rather than accept a deal you expect me to break.

You see the same structure in arms races, in security dilemmas, in all sorts of economic settings. Each side would like to be restrained, but they can't verify or enforce that the other side will be restrained too, so everyone defects.

Why does this matter for AI? A few reasons. First, AI may sharpen these dynamics among humans. If there's a perception that whoever leads in advanced AI could gain a decisive and lasting advantage, that's exactly the kind of shifting power situation where commitment problems are most dangerous. Labs or states might race and cut corners on safety, even though they'd all prefer a slower, more careful path, because nobody can credibly promise to hold back.

Second, as AI systems become agents acting in the world on behalf of people and organizations, they'll face these problems among themselves. We want AI systems that can find mutually beneficial agreements and avoid destructive conflict, rather than getting stuck in the same traps humans do, possibly at faster speeds and higher stakes.

Third, and this is the hopeful part, AI might also help solve commitment problems. You can imagine technical tools that make commitments more credible: better verification, ways of proving what a system will or won't do, institutions mediated by trustworthy systems, perhaps even agents that can make conditional commitments that others can inspect. So cooperative AI as a field is partly about avoiding new failures of cooperation and partly about using AI to build the infrastructure of trust that humans have always struggled to create.

But there's a flip side worth flagging. The ability to make credible commitments is double-edged. It also enables credible threats, coercion, and extortion. If I can bind myself to carrying out a threat, I become much more dangerous to bargain with. So the research agenda isn't simply "make commitment easier." It's figuring out how to enable the good kinds of commitment, the ones that support peace and mutual gains, without unleashing a world where everyone can lock in threats. That's a subtle problem, and I think it's one of the more underappreciated parts of the AI governance and safety picture.

r001.rationale: The response describes parties’ inability to credibly commit, but does not state that this can happen even when both know the nature of the game.

r002.rationale: It discusses defection and cooperation generally, but does not explain the one-shot prisoner’s dilemma or link defection there to the absence of enforceable conditional cooperation.

r003.rationale: It mentions possible tools for making commitments more credible, but does not clearly ask whether they can implement a cooperative bargain through each party’s credible commitment to follow it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the commitment problem is really one of the oldest and deepest problems in the study of conflict and cooperation. The basic idea comes out of bargaining theory, and the classic statement of it in international relations is from James Fearon's work on rationalist explanations for war. The puzzle is: if war is costly, and both sides know it's costly, there should always be some negotiated settlement that both parties prefer to fighting. So why do we see conflict at all?

And one of the key answers is that actors can't credibly commit to the deals they'd want to make. Suppose I'm a rising power and you're a declining one. I might sincerely promise today that I won't exploit my future strength against you. But you look at that promise and think, well, once Allan is strong, nothing is actually binding him. His incentives will have changed. So the promise is cheap talk. And because you can't trust it, you might choose to fight now, while you still have the advantage, rather than wait and be at my mercy later. The tragedy is that both of us would have preferred a peaceful arrangement, but there was no way to make it stick.

So the commitment problem is this gap between what actors would agree to and what they can actually bind themselves to. It shows up everywhere: in arms control, in civil war settlements where rebels are asked to disarm, in business contracts, in everyday relationships.

Now why do I think this is central for cooperative AI? A couple of reasons. One is that AI systems may be deployed in exactly these high-stakes strategic settings, negotiating or acting on behalf of companies, governments, individuals. And if they inherit the same commitment failures that humans have, we could see familiar bad equilibria, possibly moving faster and at larger scale.

But the more hopeful reason is that AI might actually change the structure of the commitment problem in ways humans never could. Humans are notoriously bad at credible commitment. We can't open up our heads and show someone our true intentions. But an AI system is, at least in principle, inspectable. You could imagine verification schemes where one party can check the other's model, or where two agents jointly delegate to a system whose code is transparent and whose behavior is provably constrained. That's a kind of credible commitment technology that just hasn't existed before.

Of course there's a dark side to that too. Credible commitment isn't always good. Commitment to a threat is also commitment, and if agents can credibly bind themselves to retaliate or to never back down, you can get brinkmanship that's worse than what we have now. So the research question isn't just "how do we enable commitment," it's "how do we build the capabilities and the norms so that commitment is used for mutually beneficial agreements rather than coercion."

So when I talk about cooperative AI, understanding commitment is a big piece of it. It's both a problem AI might worsen and an opportunity for AI to help solve something that's plagued human institutions for a very long time.

r001.rationale: It says both sides know war is costly yet may still fight because neither can trust the other’s promise, capturing the problem despite shared knowledge of the situation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses commitment failures generally, but does not explain how lack of enforceable conditional cooperation leads to defection in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma.

r003.rationale: It raises how to enable commitment for mutually beneficial agreements and describes verification and transparent systems that could make one party’s commitments credible to the other.

astra-6.text:
The commitment problem is that even when everyone would benefit from an agreement, they may not be able to credibly commit to carrying it out. You can sincerely want to cooperate today, but if the other side knows that tomorrow you’ll have an incentive to break the agreement, your promise may not be enough.

Imagine that one party expects to become much more powerful. They might promise to respect the other party’s interests once they’re powerful, but the other party asks, “What will actually hold you to that?” If there’s no good answer, both sides can end up taking costly defensive actions, even fighting, rather than reaching a bargain that would leave them both better off.

For cooperative AI, one question is whether we can build systems that make commitments more credible. Could a system make a limited, verifiable commitment about how it will act, without having to reveal all its private information? That could expand the agreements people can safely make. But we also need to understand the risks, because the ability to commit can be used to make threats credible as well as promises.

r001.rationale: The response says commitment problems can persist despite mutual benefit, but it does not state that the parties know the nature of the game they are playing.

r002.rationale: It describes costly defensive actions and possible fighting, but does not explain that absent enforceable conditional cooperation, agents defect in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma.

r003.rationale: It asks whether systems can make commitments more credible and thereby expand the agreements people can safely make, communicating the idea of using technology to support cooperative bargains through credible commitments.

sol-6.1.text:
The commitment problem is that sometimes actors would all prefer a cooperative outcome, but they can’t credibly commit to doing their part. Even if they sincerely intend to cooperate today, they may have an incentive to defect later, and everyone can anticipate that.

Imagine two parties considering an agreement that would make one of them much more powerful. They might both benefit from the agreement, but the party that becomes weaker has to ask: once the balance of power changes, why would the stronger party keep its promises? Simply saying, “Trust me,” doesn’t resolve that concern. So they may forgo a mutually beneficial agreement, or even end up in conflict.

For cooperative AI, the question is whether we can build systems and institutions that make commitments credible. Could an AI system help parties verify compliance, make an agreement conditional on what others do, or reliably constrain its own future behavior? The aim is to expand the set of cooperative arrangements that are actually achievable, even when the participants have different interests.

r001.rationale: The response describes anticipated incentives to defect, but does not state that the parties know the nature of the game they are playing.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible defection and unreliable promises, but does not explain that the lack of enforceable conditional cooperation causes defection in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma.

r003.rationale: It asks whether AI systems and institutions can make commitments credible and help implement cooperative agreements.
